newsitem.title: UK: TURKISH BANKS TAP EUROMARKET FOR LONGER-TERM FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: TURKISH BANKS TAP EUROMARKET FOR LONGER-TERM FUNDS.

text.p: In a bid to secure longer-dated debt, Turkish banks are turning to the Eurobond market, away from the syndicated loan market, even if it means paying a premium, bankers said on Wednesday.

The Export Credit Bank of Turkey's $200 million three-year bond launched on Wednesday was no exception, raising longer-term money for the borrower, said underwriter of the transaction Salomon Brothers.

"There's a desire on the part of Turkish financial institutions to access longer-term funding as the bulk of the syndicated loan market has been one-year debt," Salomon Brothers syndicate manager Michael Ridley said.
The Turkish banking sector is one of the syndicated loan market's more active sources of business.
The deal follows a $150 million five-year transaction for Turkey's largest private bank Yapi Kredi that was priced to yield 395 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes.
Export Credit Bank Turkey, known as Turk Eximbank, is the only Turkish financial institution with the same ratings as the sovereign of B1 by Moody's Investors Service and B by Standard and Poor's.
"We roadshowed a couple of weeks ago and developed demand for both fixed and floating rate bonds, so we decided to launch a two-tranche bond," Ridley said.
Both tranches mature in August 2000, with one tranche paying a 9.0-percent fixed-rate coupon and the other tranche paying 250 basis points over six-month LIBOR.
Ridley said the sales distribution was broad-based with demand from Britain, Japan, Korea, Switzerland, offshore U.S. accounts and the Middle East.
In May, Turk Eximbank set a one-year syndicated loan which was priced 75 b.p. over LIBOR, or at an all-in spread of 125 b.p. over.
